faq.q: What makes the sound of thunder?
faq.a: Lightning heats the air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius in a fraction of a second. The air expands explosively, making a shock wave that we hear as thunder.
asks: Why does lightning make a noise?

faq.q: How can I tell how far away a storm is?
faq.a: Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, then divide by three for kilometres, or by five for miles. If the gap is getting shorter, the storm is coming closer.
asks: How do you count the distance of lightning?

faq.a: A lightning bolt can be kilometres long. Sound from the nearest part reaches you first and sound from the farthest part arrives seconds later, so the noise rolls on. Echoes from hills and clouds add to it.
asks: Why is thunder a long rumble?

faq.q: Can there be lightning without thunder?
faq.a: Every lightning bolt makes thunder, but thunder usually cannot be heard more than about 15 to 20 kilometres away. Distant flashes with no sound are sometimes called heat lightning.
Thunder itself is just sound and cannot hurt you. But hearing it means lightning is close enough to strike, so it is time to go indoors.

facts: Sound travels about 343 metres per second in air at 20 degrees Celsius.
Thunder can rarely be heard more than about 15 to 20 kilometres from the lightning.

quiz.say: You see lightning and hear the thunder 9 seconds later. About how far away was it?
quiz.show: Flash, then thunder 9 seconds later. How far?
quiz.why: Sound travels about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds, so 9 seconds means about 3 kilometres.

wrong.0: 1 kilometre would be a gap of about 3 seconds.
wrong.2: That counts one kilometre per second, but sound takes about 3 seconds per kilometre.
